summary:
Banni, in Kachchh, India, is Asia’s largest tropical grassland and home to about 40,000 Maldhari herders. Satellites show it greening since 2001 — but recovering pasture, an invasive shrub and a run of wet monsoons all look identical from orbit.

GlobalClimateLens asks the harder question: after we remove rainfall, is anything still rising? Using NASA MODIS greenness and GPM IMERG rainfall through Google Earth Engine, we apply residual trend analysis to 2001–2024. Rainfall explains about two thirds of the greening. The remaining third keeps rising at +0.0017 NDVI per year (p = 0.006), and holds under a second satellite, a second vegetation index, several rainfall formulations and a change of analysis window.

The platform reports this in two modes — a full scientific paper for researchers, and a plain-language animated explainer for students and the communities who live there. Every number is computed from the stored NASA series; nothing is hard-coded. We also state plainly what a satellite cannot settle: Prosopis invasion, groundwater, dams and salinity need ground data. The result tells you how much, and exactly where to go measure why.
details:
What Global Climate Lens

GlobalClimateLens is an open Earth-observation platform with two jobs: it tests what satellite data can and cannot prove about long-term land change, and it explains that result in plain language to the people who live on that land. Our case study is the Banni Grasslands of Kachchh, Gujarat, India (2001-2024), Asia's largest tropical grassland and home to roughly 40,000 Maldhari pastoralists.

The finding, stated first

Banni has greened by about +0.005 NDVI per year since 2001. Monsoon rainfall explains about two thirds of that rise. The remaining third is not noise: after the rainfall signal is removed, greenness is still climbing at +0.0017 NDVI per year, with p = 0.006 on a Hamed-Rao corrected Mann-Kendall test. We replayed the 24 years one thousand times with no underlying trend and only 6 replays produced a residual this large. Something other than rain is changing this land, and we can say how much. We cannot say what it is, and we explain exactly why not.

The problem we set out to detect

In a dryland, greener is not automatically better. Recovering pasture, a run of wet monsoons, and the invasive shrub Prosopis juliflora all produce the same green pixels. Prosopis was planted in Banni by the Gujarat forest department in 1961 to hold back the advancing salt desert. It spread instead, and today covers close to half the grassland. The Maldharis adapted: charcoal made from Prosopis wood is now the second most important occupation in Banni after buffalo pastoralism. That adaptation hides the damage. A landscape can look greener every year on satellite imagery while the grass that feeds the buffalo economy shrinks beneath it, because the shrub replacing the grass is itself green, and because the income from burning it masks the loss. So we asked a sharper question than "is Banni greening?" We asked: after rainfall is removed, is anything still rising?

How it works

Monsoon-season greenness (MODIS NDVI, 250 m) over a 9,751 square kilometre window is regressed on that year's GPM IMERG monsoon rainfall (r = 0.91, R-squared = 0.83). We remove the rainfall signal and test what remains using residual trend analysis (RESTREND) with a Theil-Sen slope, a Hamed-Rao corrected Mann-Kendall test, and bootstrap confidence intervals.

How hard we tried to break it

A single favourable result is not evidence, so we attacked it. The residual keeps the same sign and a similar size under a second satellite (Aqua MYD13Q1), a second vegetation index (EVI), several different rainfall formulations, four different analysis rectangles, and a change of analysis window. It is present outside the monsoon season as well. We also reproduced the headline statistics in two independent implementations, server-side Python and in-browser JavaScript, and they agree. The standard assumption that a rising dryland NDVI trend simply reflects favourable rainfall is therefore not sufficient for Banni.

What we deliberately do not claim

We tested the candidate causes one by one. Rainfall is confirmed. Sensor change, rainfall timing within the season, and cropland expansion were each tested and eliminated. Four candidates - Prosopis invasion, groundwater change, upstream dams and soil salinity - cannot be settled from orbit at all, because NDVI measures greenness, not species, and a dense Prosopis thicket is as green as healthy pasture. So we name no cause. Naming one would be the easy, unprovable answer. Instead the platform states how large the unexplained signal is, how confident we are, and exactly which ground measurements would settle it: Central Ground Water Board well records, a field-trained Prosopis extent map, and fodder surveys with Maldhari households.

Who benefits

If the unexplained greening is recovering pasture, Banni's restoration policy is working and should continue. If it is shrub invasion, the fodder base of 40,000 herders is shrinking while the satellite record looks healthier every year. Any policy that monitors drylands by greenness alone carries this blind spot. Existing research finds that controlling Prosopis would benefit both the ecology of Banni and pastoralist livelihoods; our contribution is measured evidence that a non-rainfall change is underway, and its scale. For the Forest Department and for NGOs working with Maldhari communities, that converts a vague concern into a budgeted field survey.

Making it understandable, not just correct

A result nobody outside a lab can read has no impact, so we built the explanation into the product.

The live site opens on an Overview scene that plays the full 24-year record as a single illustration: rain falls from the clouds and the ground beneath it changes colour year by year, both driven by the stored NASA series rather than by hand-set artwork. Move through the years and a dry monsoon visibly thins the rain and fades the vegetation; a strong monsoon fills both. A single control switches the rain off entirely, leaving only the greenness that rainfall does not explain - the drought view. That one toggle is the whole method in a form a schoolchild can operate: this is the land with rain, this is the land with rain removed, and the difference is what our study measures.

Beyond it, the platform runs in two modes from the same computed numbers. Research mode is the full paper: study-area map, methodology, statistical tables, figures with 95 percent confidence intervals, limitations, references and data exports. Student and Community mode carries every conclusion of the research in ordinary language with no equations - a U-tube that shows how greenness follows rainfall, a see-saw that shows what a residual is, an NDVI colour scale that names what bare, sparse and dense ground look like, and a thousand dots that show what p = 0.006 actually means. A school student and a reviewer see the same numbers, explained at different depths.

How it is built

Python and FastAPI backend, React and TypeScript frontend, all datasets accessed through Google Earth Engine, deployed as a container on Microsoft Azure. Nothing is hard-coded: every number on screen is computed from the stored NASA series when the page loads, so the simple mode can never drift from the scientific one.

What our team considered

Team member Purnendu Shukla, based in Gujarat, contributed local ground context and regional reporting that shaped which causes we chose to test. Our central design decision was to make the project's honesty visible rather than buried: limitations are a first-class page on the platform, not a footnote.

Limitations

The analysis window is a rectangle, not the exact Banni administrative polygon; we verified the trend is statistically indistinguishable inside and outside it and across four sub-rectangles, but it remains a regional measure. Twenty-four annual values is a short series, so every figure carries a confidence interval. NDVI cannot distinguish plant species.

Next steps

Central Ground Water Board well records for Kachchh, a field-trained Prosopis extent map for an early epoch compared with today, and on-site water-use and fodder measurements with Maldhari communities and the Gujarat Forest Department.
